## Setup

- If you don't have it already, get the Stata formatted version of the ANES data.

- Run `install.packages(c("srvyr", "survey"))`

## Setup

Once you've got the packages installed, and the data downloaded, you can use the code below to import/cleanup the ANES 2024 data:

```{r}

library(tidyverse)
library(gtsummary)
library(gt)
library(survey)
library(srvyr)
fname<-here::here("data", "anes_timeseries_2024_stata_20250808.zip")
missing<-c("-9. Refused", "-8. Don't know","-4. Error", "-1. Inapplicable" )
anes  <- haven::read_dta(fname)|>
  # converting feeling thermometer questions to numeric
  mutate(across(c(V241156:V241168, 
                  V241712:V241720,
                  V242125:V242156,
                  V242514:V242518
                  ),  .fns=~if_else(.x>=0 & .x<=100, as.numeric(.x), NA)))|>
  # converting all other variables to factors
  as_factor()|>
  filter(V240002c == "2. Completed pre and post-election interviews")|>
  mutate(across(where(is.factor), 
                .fns=~fct_collapse(.x, "Missing" = missing)|>
                  fct_recode(NULL = "Missing")|>
                  fct_drop()))



# getting the list of question labels
question_labels<-lapply(anes, function(x) attr(x, "label"))


```


## Note on the setup


- We previously used .csv formatted files, but we're using a file with the `.dta` extension for this class.

- `.dta` is the format used by Stata software. Stata formatted files have some additional features that a .csv can't have. Most importantly, they can include a question label and value labels for each variable.

- This mainly means that we don't have to recode *as much* to run analyses.



## Reading methodology documents

### What we need

You'll always need to identify the weighting variable. If you can't find this, then none of this other advice applies.

### What we need

Other than weights, there are three additional features than *might* be present depending on the survey:

-   **Primary Sampling Unit (PSU)**: in clustered samples, the PSU indicates the first "clustering" characteristic sampled. Note that many surveys have multiple stages of clustering, so there can be secondary or tertiary sampling units as well, but these may not be reported.

-   **Strata IDs**: Surveys that use stratified samples will often include a unique identifier for each strata.

-   **Target population size** some surveys will include a rough estimate of the size of their target population. Where this is included, you can use it to apply the finite population correction.

### Weighted proportions in R

If we're just interested in calculating simple weighted proportions or counts, we can just use the `weight` variable alone.


```{r}
#| code-fold: true
question<-"In the past 12 months: have you joined a protest march, rally, or demonstration?"
anes |>
  as_factor()|>
  mutate(protest = V242029) |>
  drop_na(V240107b, protest)|>
  group_by(protest)|>
  summarize( n = n(),
             weighted.n = sum(V240107b)
             )|>
  mutate(percent = n/sum(n),
         weighted.percent = weighted.n/sum(weighted.n)
         )|>
  gt()|>
  cols_align(align='left')|>
  fmt_integer(columns = c(n, weighted.n))|>
  fmt_percent(columns = c(percent, weighted.percent))

```

... But calculating variance (and thus confidence intervals and p.values) for a complex survey is tricky, which is why we use specialized packages.

### R packages for complex surveys


-   The R packages `survey` and `srvyr` offer a suite of tools for handling these calculations.

-   The `gtsummary` package has some built-in shortcuts for creating formatted tables from survey data.

### Declaring a survey design in srvyr
::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- To start, we need to convert a conventional tibble or dataframe into a survey design object using `as_survey_design`. 

- Once we do this, we can use `srvyr` functions on it and the weights and variance calculations will be performed automatically.

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
# Example of general syntax:
survey_object <- svy_data |>
  as_survey_design(id = psu,
                   weights = weighting_var,
                   strata = strata_id)

```
:::
:::::



### Declaring a survey design in srvyr

::::::::: columns
::::::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment data-code-focus="1"}
-   `svy_data` is the original data set
:::

::: {.fragment data-code-focus="2"}
-   `id` should be the name of the primary sampling unit variable.
:::

::: {.fragment data-code-focus="3"}
-   `weight` should be the name of the weighting variable.
:::

::: {.fragment data-code-focus="4"}
-   `strata` should be the strata variable.
:::
:::::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
The basic syntax will look like this:

```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
survey_object <- svy_data |>
  as_survey_design(id = psu,
                   weights = weighting_var,
                   strata = strata_id)

```
:::
:::::::::

### Declaring a survey design in srvyr

Here's how we can set this up for the ANES data

::: {.fragment data-code-focus="1-6"}
:::


:::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.fragment data-code-focus="2"}
-   Respondents who skipped the post-election round of the ANES have missing weights. Dropping these avoids an error.
:::

::: {.fragment data-code-focus="6"}
-   `nest=TRUE` some relabeling so that the cluster IDs are unique to each strata. (If you need this, R will tell you with an error message.)
:::
:::::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
anes_survey <- anes |>
  drop_na(V240108b) |>
  as_survey_design(ids = V240108c,
                   weight = V240108b,
                   strata = V240108d,
                   nest = TRUE
                   )


```
:::

::: {.fragment data-code-focus="1-6"}
Now we should use the `anes_survey` object to analyze the survey.
:::
::::::::


### Basic steps

- `srvyr` is modeled on the `dplyr` syntax you've already used, so things like `group_by` and `summarise` will work more-or-less the same way.


- Most of the important functions will only work when paired with `summarise` and/or `group_by`

### survey_prop



```{r, eval=FALSE}
survey_mean(
   x,
   na.rm = FALSE,
   vartype = c("se", "ci", "var", "cv"),
   level = 0.95,
   proportion = FALSE,
   prop_method = c("logit", "likelihood", "asin", "beta", "mean"),
   deff = FALSE,
   df = NULL,
   ...
)

```

```{r, eval=FALSE}
survey_prop(
  vartype = c("se", "ci", "var", "cv"),
  level = 0.95,
  proportion = FALSE,
  prop_method = c("logit", "likelihood", "asin", "beta", "mean"),
  deff = FALSE,
  df = NULL,
  ...
)
```

### survey_prop

You can use `survey_prop` to calculate proportions along levels of a grouping variable.

```{r}
# In the past 12 months: have you joined a protest march, rally, or demonstration?
anes_survey|>
  group_by(V242029)|>
  summarise(survey_prop(),      # weighted proportions
            n = unweighted(n()) # unweighted counts
            )
  
  


```


### survey_prop


`vartype="ci"` will report a 95% confidence interval instead of the standard error:

```{r}
# In the past 12 months: have you joined a protest march, rally, or demonstration?
anes_survey|>
  group_by(V242029)|>
  summarise(survey_prop(vartype = "ci"),      # weighted proportions
            n = unweighted(n()) # unweighted counts
            )
  


```

### survey_prop

I can get proportions along multiple categories by adding a second grouping variable. Note that these proportions sum to 1 for the first variable listed

```{r}
# V241235: How much do you feel that having elections makes the government pay attention?
# V242029: In the past 12 months: have you joined a protest march, rally, or demonstration?
anes_survey|>
  group_by(V241235, V242029)|>
  summarise(survey_prop(vartype = "ci"),      # weighted proportions
            n = unweighted(n()) # unweighted counts
            )|>
  drop_na()
  


```


### survey_mean


`survey_mean` will report the average for a numeric variable. Note that I need to use `na.rm=T` here for the same reasons I typically need it when calculating a regular average. 

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

#V242141 Average feeling thermometer towards big businesses:
anes_survey|>
  summarise(`big_business_therm` = survey_mean(V242141 , 
                                               vartype = "ci",
                                               na.rm=T),
            n = unweighted(n()) # unweighted counts
            )
  


```

### survey_mean

Pairing `survey_mean` with `group_by` will return an average for each value of the grouping variable:

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

# V241497 : Does R belong to a labor union?

anes_survey|>
  group_by(V241497)|>
  summarise(`big_business_therm` = survey_mean(V242141 , 
                                               vartype = "ci",
                                               na.rm=T),      # weighted proportions
            n = unweighted(n()) # unweighted counts
            )|>
  drop_na()
  

```


### Difference of means test

We can use the `svyttest` function from the `survey` package to calculate a difference of means test examining the relationship between labor union membership (V241497) and feelings towards big business (V242141)


```{r}
#| code-fold: true

library(survey)
svyttest(formula = V242141 ~V241497 ,
         design = anes_survey,
         na.rm=T
         )

```

### Using gtsummary

`gtsummary` has some additional functions for working with survey data objects. The `tbl_svysummary` function will automatically report weighted proportions and variances for survey objects:


```{r, cache=TRUE}
#| code-fold: true

anes_survey|>
  tbl_svysummary(include =V242029)|>
  # add confidence intervals
  add_ci()
  
```

### Using gtsummary


Using `add_p()` on a cross tab will automatically calculate a $\chi^2$ p-value, which gives us a probability of seeing these disproportionalities if the row and column variables are unrelated:

```{r, cache=TRUE}
#| code-fold: true

anes_survey|>
  drop_na(V241235, V241407)|>
  tbl_svysummary(include =V241235, by =V241407)|>
  add_p()
  
```

### Using gtsummary

This also works for continuous variables:

```{r, cache=TRUE}
#| code-fold: true

anes_survey|>
  drop_na(V242141, V241497)|>
  tbl_svysummary(include =V242141,  by= V241497,
                 label = list(V242141= "Feeling thermometer towards big business")

                 )|>
  modify_spanning_header(
    all_stat_cols() ~ "Do you or anyone else in this household belong to a labor union or to
an employee association similar to a union?"
  )

```

### Using gtsummary

`add_p()` with this table will add a p-value for a Kruskal-Wallis test, which tests the null hypothesis that the continuous variable has the same mean across all categories.

```{r, cache=TRUE}
#| code-fold: true

anes_survey|>
  drop_na(V242141, V241497)|>
  
  tbl_svysummary(include =V242141,  by= V241497,
                 label = list(V242141= "Feeling thermometer towards big business")

                 )|>
  modify_spanning_header(
    all_stat_cols() ~ "Do you or anyone else in this household belong to a labor union or to
an employee association similar to a union?"
  )|>
  add_p()

```


## Using gtsummary

However, we can use `add_difference()` to calculate a difference of means test, and we can add this argument: `statistic = V242141 ~ "{mean} ({sd})"` to show the mean and standard deviation instead of the median.

```{r}
#| code-fold: true

anes_survey|>
  drop_na(V242141, V241497)|>
  
  tbl_svysummary(include =V242141,  by= V241497,
                 label = list(V242141= "Feeling thermometer towards big business"),
                 statistic = V242141 ~ "{mean} ({sd})"

                 )|>
  modify_spanning_header(
    all_stat_cols() ~ "Do you or anyone else in this household belong to a labor union or to
an employee association similar to a union?"
  )|>
  add_difference()

```
